concepts.name: Maxwell’s equations
concepts.statement: Maxwell gathered the work of Oersted, Coulomb, Gauss and Faraday into four statements that together make a complete theory of electricity and magnetism. Electric field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative ones. Magnetic field lines have no beginning and no end. A changing magnetic field induces an electric field. Moving charges and changing electric fields make magnetic fields. Everything else in this chapter follows from these four.

concepts.name: Changing electric field as a source of magnetism
concepts.statement: Faraday had shown that a changing magnetic field makes an electric field. Maxwell added the symmetric statement, that a changing electric field makes a magnetic field, and this addition is what turns four separate laws into a theory that predicts a wave. Each field, in changing, creates the other, so a disturbance can keep itself going and travel away from whatever started it. Without this one hypothesis there is no electromagnetic wave to predict.

concepts.name: Speed of an electromagnetic wave
concepts.statement: Maxwell's theory does not merely say that a wave exists; it says how fast the wave goes. It gives that speed from two constants measured in the laboratory with charges and with currents, which have nothing to do with light. The permittivity of free space sets the strength of the electric force and the permeability of free space sets the strength of the magnetic force. The square root of their product sets the one speed at which the two fields can carry each other along.

concepts.name: Light as an electromagnetic wave
concepts.statement: The speed Maxwell calculated from two electrical constants is the speed of light, and a coincidence of that size is not a coincidence. Maxwell concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave of the particular wavelengths the eye happens to detect. The conclusion carries a prediction with it: if light is one band of a wave, other wavelengths should exist and should be findable, and the whole of the next two sections is spent on them.

concepts.name: Hertz’s observations
concepts.statement: A prediction is worth what its test is worth. Starting in 1887, Hertz drove a loop of wire from a circuit resonating at a known frequency, so that sparks jumped a gap in it, and set a second tuned loop across the laboratory, where sparks also appeared. He then measured the wavelength from the interference patterns, and since he knew the frequency, he could find the speed from $v = f\lambda$ and show that it was the speed of light. The SI unit of frequency carries his name.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic wave
concepts.statement: An electromagnetic wave is a pair of changing electric and magnetic fields that generate each other and travel together through space, carrying energy, at the speed of light in a vacuum.

concepts.name: Hertz
concepts.statement: The hertz is the SI unit of frequency, one cycle per second, named for Heinrich Hertz, who first generated and detected electromagnetic waves.

concepts.name: Radiation from accelerated charges
concepts.statement: Whenever a current varies, the electric and magnetic fields around it vary, and the variation moves out from the source as a wave. The general statement is simpler still: accelerating charges radiate. That is why an alternating source drives a broadcast antenna, why an unshielded circuit leaks energy, and why a microwave oven has an antenna carrying an oscillating current.

concepts.name: Antenna electric field over one cycle
concepts.statement: An alternating source at the centre of a straight wire drives charge to one end and then to the other. At the instant of greatest separation, the electric field beside the antenna is greatest. A quarter of a cycle later the charges have met in the middle and the field there is zero, while the earlier maximum has already travelled away at $\kc$. One full cycle shows where the wave's shape comes from. How far the charges separate sets its amplitude, and how long the source takes to complete a cycle sets its wavelength, so a high frequency makes a short wave.

concepts.name: Magnetic part of the wave
concepts.statement: The same charges that separate along the antenna are a current while they move, and by Ampere's law a current makes a magnetic field, whose lines circle the wire. As the current varies, that field varies with it and propagates away at the speed of light, exactly as the electric field does. The magnetic part has the same period and the same wavelength as the electric part, because the same motion of the same charges makes both.

concepts.name: Transverse electromagnetic wave
concepts.statement: The two fields of the wave lie in different planes. The electric field oscillates in one plane, the magnetic field in a plane at right angles to it, and the wave travels along the line where the two planes meet. Both fields are therefore perpendicular to the direction of propagation, which makes an electromagnetic wave transverse. The two are also exactly in phase: they reach their maxima together and pass through zero together. This arrangement decides how a wave couples to a receiving wire or loop, so learn to picture it from any angle.

concepts.name: Ratio of field strengths
concepts.statement: The stronger the electric field made by the separated charge, the greater the current that flows and so the greater the magnetic field, so the two field strengths ought to rise and fall together. They do, and the constant ratio between them is the speed of light itself, at every instant and at every point in space. Because $\kc$ is such a large number, the result also says that the magnetic part of any electromagnetic wave is very weak beside the electric part.

concepts.name: Finding one field strength from the other
concepts.statement: Rearranging the ratio gives either field from the other in one step, and this is the calculation the section's problems ask for over and over. Dividing a field of 1000 V/m by the speed of light leaves a few microtesla, less than a tenth of the Earth's own weak field, which is the concrete form of the statement that the magnetic part of a wave is small. Checking that the units of volts per metre divided by metres per second really are teslas is worth doing once.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic wave in a medium
concepts.statement: Outside a vacuum an electromagnetic wave is slower, by the factor the medium's index of refraction names. The ratio of the field strengths is reduced in exactly the same proportion, so in a medium it is the wave's own speed, not the speed of light, that the two fields stand in. The result matters wherever a wave is not travelling through empty space, which is most of the places a reader will meet one.

concepts.name: Antenna resonance
concepts.statement: An antenna is not a circuit with a complete path. It is a wire on which the driving source sets up a standing wave of charge, and its dimensions decide the frequency at which it radiates best. That is a resonance, and tuning a radio or a television means changing electrical properties until the resonant condition is met. A receiving antenna works the same way in reverse. An arriving wave accelerates the electrons in it and sets up a standing wave that the set amplifies, so it too must resonate at the frequencies it should catch.

concepts.name: Oscillation
concepts.statement: To oscillate is to fluctuate back and forth in a steady beat, as the charges in an antenna do and as the fields of the wave they send out do.

concepts.name: Wave equation for light
concepts.statement: Propagation speed, frequency and wavelength are related for any wave by $\kvw = \kf\klam$, and for an electromagnetic wave in a vacuum the propagation speed is always the speed of light. Since $\kc$ never changes, the frequency and the wavelength can only trade against each other: the greater the frequency, the smaller the wavelength. This one relation is what lets the whole spectrum be laid out on a single axis and read in either unit.

concepts.name: Finding a wavelength or frequency
concepts.statement: Rearranged, the relation gives $\klam = \kc/\kf$, and this is the arithmetic that most of the section's problems come down to. An AM carrier of 1530 kHz is nearly 200 m long, an FM carrier of 105.1 MHz is 2.85 m, and a cell phone's 1.90 GHz signal is 15.8 cm; those three numbers explain why an AM mast is enormous and a phone's antenna is hidden inside the case. Carrying the units through as cycles per second keeps the answer in metres.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic spectrum
concepts.statement: All electromagnetic waves are the same phenomenon, and only frequency, and therefore wavelength, separates a radio wave from a gamma ray. Sorting them by frequency gives the named bands, radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma ray, over a remarkable range of frequencies and wavelengths. Some of the dividing lines are sharp and others are not. Where two bands overlap, the name of a wave depends on how it was made rather than on how fast it oscillates.

concepts.name: Rules of thumb for the spectrum
concepts.statement: Three statements hold across the whole spectrum and are worth carrying: a higher-frequency wave is more energetic and penetrates better, a higher-frequency wave carries more information in a given time, and the shorter the wavelength of a wave used to probe something, the smaller the detail it can resolve. Each has exceptions — magnetic resonance imaging uses 3 m radio waves to see detail smaller than a millimetre — and knowing that the rules are rules of thumb is part of knowing them.

concepts.name: Transmission, reflection and absorption
concepts.statement: When a wave meets a material, it may pass through, turn back, or be absorbed, and usually some of each happens. How a material behaves depends on the material and the frequency together, not on the material alone. Glass passes visible light and stops ultraviolet, and skin stops visible light and passes X-rays. A substance is transparent or opaque only for a named band.

concepts.name: Radio waves and modulation
concepts.statement: Radio waves are defined by their source: any electromagnetic wave produced by currents in wires and circuits is one. To carry information, a station varies a carrier at its own frequency, either in amplitude, which is AM, or in frequency, which is FM. The receiver resonates at the carrier frequency and responds to whichever kind of variation it uses. Noise adds to amplitude, so an FM receiver can throw away what an AM receiver must treat as part of the signal, which makes FM the quieter of the two.

concepts.name: Most efficient antenna length
concepts.statement: An antenna radiates best when a standing wave fits on it, and for a linear antenna that length is $\klam/2$. With one end on the ground, a quarter wavelength does the same work, just as a tube closed at one end resonates at a quarter of its fundamental wavelength. The rule explains the sizes of antennas you see. An AM broadcast antenna must be hundreds of metres long, while an FM or mobile phone antenna is small enough to hide and goes high up for a clear line of sight.

concepts.name: Uses of microwaves
concepts.statement: Microwaves are the highest frequencies that currents in ordinary circuits can produce, from about $10^{9}$ Hz up to the highest practical $LC$ resonance near $10^{12}$ Hz, and their short wavelengths make them good for carrying information and for seeing detail. Radar finds a distance by timing an echo and a speed by the Doppler shift in it, and maps a planet through cloud that stops visible light. In a microwave oven the frequency is chosen so that polar molecules turning to follow the alternating field absorb the energy, which heats the food and not the plate, and the hot spots are an interference pattern.

concepts.name: Sources across the spectrum
concepts.statement: Each band comes from a process of a particular size. Accelerating charges in circuits give radio waves and microwaves. The thermal agitation of atoms and molecules, and their vibrations and rotations, give microwaves, infrared and some visible light. Electronic transitions within atoms and molecules give visible light and ultraviolet. Transitions of inner electrons and the braking of fast electrons in matter give X-rays, and the nucleus itself gives gamma rays. The source decides the name where two bands overlap, since an X-ray and a gamma ray of the same frequency differ only in origin.

concepts.name: Radiation and living tissue
concepts.statement: The higher the frequency, the more energy a wave delivers to whatever absorbs it, and above visible light that energy begins to break molecules apart. Ultraviolet-B excites and distorts DNA and causes skin cancer and cataracts, and the ozone layer is what keeps most of it off the surface; X-rays penetrate further and damage more, which is both their hazard and, aimed carefully, their use against cancer; gamma rays do the same at higher energies. The same properties make them useful: sterilization, vitamin D, imaging by shadow and by emission, and therapy.

concepts.name: Thermal agitation
concepts.statement: Thermal agitation is the thermal motion of the atoms and molecules of any object above absolute zero, which makes them emit and absorb radiation, mostly in the infrared.

concepts.name: Infrared radiation
concepts.statement: Infrared radiation is the band of the electromagnetic spectrum with frequencies from just below those of red light down to the microwaves.

concepts.name: Visible light
concepts.statement: Visible light is the narrow band of the electromagnetic spectrum to which the normal human eye responds, with wavelengths from about 380 nm to 760 nm.

concepts.name: Ultraviolet radiation
concepts.statement: Ultraviolet radiation is the band of the electromagnetic spectrum extending upward in frequency from violet light and overlapping the lowest x rays.

concepts.name: X rays
concepts.statement: X rays are invisible, penetrating electromagnetic radiation of very high frequency, overlapping the ultraviolet below and the gamma rays above.

concepts.name: Gamma rays
concepts.statement: Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation of extremely high frequency, emitted by the nucleus of an atom in nuclear decay or in other nuclear and particle processes.

concepts.name: Carrier wave
concepts.statement: A carrier wave is an electromagnetic wave that carries a signal by the modulation of its amplitude or of its frequency.

concepts.name: Amplitude modulation
concepts.statement: Amplitude modulation places information on an electromagnetic wave by varying the amplitude of a carrier wave with the signal, while its frequency stays fixed.

concepts.name: Frequency modulation
concepts.statement: Frequency modulation places information on an electromagnetic wave by varying the frequency of a carrier wave with the signal, while its amplitude stays fixed.

concepts.name: Radar
concepts.statement: Radar is a common application of microwaves: it finds the distance to objects as diverse as clouds and aircraft from the time a reflected pulse takes to return.

concepts.name: Extremely low frequency
concepts.statement: Extremely low frequency radiation is electromagnetic radiation of the lowest frequencies, usually from 0 to 300 Hz but also up to about 1 kHz.

concepts.name: Television
concepts.statement: Television carries video and audio signals on electromagnetic waves, broadcast in the radio band.

concepts.name: Very high frequency
concepts.statement: Very high frequency TV channels use frequencies in the two ranges from 54 to 88 MHz and from 174 to 222 MHz.

concepts.name: Ultra-high frequency
concepts.statement: Ultra-high frequency TV channels use frequencies above those of VHF, from 470 to 1000 MHz.

concepts.name: Wave energy and field amplitude
concepts.statement: A wave brings energy into a system because its fields exert forces on charges and move them, and the larger the fields, the more work they can do. For waves of every kind the energy goes as the amplitude squared, and for an electromagnetic wave the amplitude is the maximum field strength, so the energy goes as $\kEfo^2$ and as $\kBmago^2$. Doubling the fields quadruples the energy, which is the whole content of the section's first figure and the reason a microwave oven with half the field takes four times as long.

concepts.name: Average intensity from the electric amplitude
concepts.statement: Intensity is power per unit area, and for a continuous sinusoidal electromagnetic wave you can write it from the electric amplitude alone. The factor of a half comes from averaging the square of a sine over a cycle, and the speed of light and the permittivity of free space turn a field strength into a power per square metre. Use this form when the electric field is the quantity given or wanted.

concepts.name: Average intensity from the magnetic amplitude
concepts.statement: Substituting $\kBmag = \kEf/\kc$ and $\varepsilon_0 = 1/\mu_0\kc^2$ into the first expression gives the intensity in terms of the magnetic amplitude, and substituting only part of the way gives it in terms of both amplitudes at once. The three forms are not three results but one, written in whichever quantities a problem happens to supply, and the principle behind all three is the same: energy in a wave is related to amplitude squared.

concepts.name: Peak intensity
concepts.statement: The three expressions are written for a sinusoidal wave, and averaging the square of a sine over a cycle leaves half of its maximum. So the intensity at the crest of the wave is twice the average intensity the same expressions give, and a problem that asks for a peak rather than an average needs the factor of two. The same factor is why the root mean square field is the amplitude divided by the square root of two.

concepts.name: Finding field amplitudes from intensity
concepts.statement: The common problem of the section runs in one direction: a source of known power spreads it over a known area, which gives the intensity, and the intensity gives the electric amplitude by rearranging the first expression, after which dividing by the speed of light gives the magnetic amplitude. Doing it in that order avoids the awkward constants twice over, and the answers are worth a glance for size, since a kilowatt in an oven gives a field of a few kilovolts per metre and a few microtesla.

concepts.name: Maximum field strength
concepts.statement: The maximum field strength of an electromagnetic wave is the amplitude of its electric or magnetic field, the largest value the field reaches as it oscillates.
